In this post, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment.","image":["https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/images/4zrzovbb/website/97d61b79f99af31d2596eced7533e6d5e3ef7731-2000x1125.jpg"],"datePublished":"2026-10-23T00:00:00.000Z","dateModified":"2026-10-23T14:51:41.000Z","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Anthropic","url":"https://www.anthropic.com"},"publisher":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Anthropic","url":"https://www.anthropic.com"},"mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-ukaisi","url":"https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-ukaisi"}Chapter 01: Alignment assessment summaryAn alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident01Alignment assessment summary02Methods03Deep dive into the primary transcript04What happened in the other eight transcripts?05DiscussionPublished

On August 4, 2026, the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) published a report that detailed some concerning behavior it observed from Claude Mythos 5 during its testing of the model’s cyber capabilities. In AISI’s evaluation, Mythos 5 was given a capture-the-flag (CTF) cybersecurity challenge, in which it was asked to retrieve a protected piece of data (the “flag”) from a simulated network. Internet access was deliberately enabled (this was standard for AISI’s cyber testing at the time, but is no longer). The cyber safeguards we deploy with general release models like Fable 5 were disabled. In nine of AISI’s 43 evaluation runs, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions (i.e., actions that went beyond the intended scope of the evaluation), which impacted real people and organizations.

In this post, which is being published alongside an independent report from AISI, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment. Like AISI’s report, we concentrate on the transcript (the complete record of the model’s reasoning and actions) from a single evaluation run. In this run:

This behavior would have been flagged immediately by our production safeguards on Fable 5, had they been enabled. Nevertheless, this behavior is important to study because the underlying failures here are not necessarily specific to cyber incidents like these. They speak to wider issues with the model’s conduct in evaluation settings; our models’ desired behavior remains a critical part of how we intend to ensure they behave responsibly.

The other eight transcripts were similar to the one described above. In each case, Claude Mythos 5 departed from the intended method for completing a CTF task, and took actions that impacted the real world. From an alignment perspective, we judge the primary transcript (above) to be equally severe or more severe than these other eight. In particular, the primary transcript showed the greatest degree of deception, in the form of Mythos 5’s attempts at social engineering to get its code change approved. Given this (and the degree of the transcripts’ similarities otherwise), we focused on completing one more exhaustive review of the primary transcript, and reviewed the other eight transcripts in less detail. This allowed us to run a large volume of experiments on the primary transcript, and thereby understand the root causes of the issues in more detail. We replayed the transcript from various points, and experimented with altering parts of the model’s prior context to examine how new information would have impacted the model’s behavior.

We judge Claude Mythos 5’s misalignment in the primary transcript to be comparable in severity to the Mythos 5 incident we discussed on September 9, in which the model uploaded a malicious package to PyPi during another CTF task. This assessment is based on our judgment of the model’s behavior in two respects: overreach, or how far the model went beyond the intended scope of the task, and dishonesty, or the extent to which the model misrepresented its actions or intentions.

On overreach, the misalignment in this incident was somewhat less severe than in the PyPi incident. Here, before it turned to an attack, Claude Mythos 5 tried several approaches that would have been within the intended scope of the task; a task misconfiguration made it difficult (or potentially impossible) for the model to pursue those within-scope solutions successfully.

On dishonesty, however, Mythos 5 went further than in the PyPi incident. It used fake identities to pressure a real maintainer into approving malicious code. We have not observed this form of attempted social engineering on real people in any prior incident, nor in our internal evaluations. We interpret this as a severe form of dishonesty, rather than some new form or category of misalignment: as in the September 9 incident, Mythos 5 used these tactics exclusively in pursuit of its assigned task, and did not pursue any goals of its own devising.

On both overreach and dishonesty, we consider the primary incident to be more severe than any of the cases described in our October 9 post. And, for context, this incident is of a very different nature to the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident that was recently investigated by OpenAI and METR. That incident saw several unique misaligned behaviors (like very large-scale coordination between agents to attack a production system), though it did not see a model trying to deceive an individual human in the same way.

Newer models appear substantially less likely to initiate the attack described here. We replayed the incident transcript with Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, and a general purpose internal research model that shows capabilities greater than Mythos 5.1. Those three models began the attack between 0% and 13% of the time, relative to 83% for Mythos 5. Our newest models also proved to be much less likely to continue the attack once they realized it was causing real-world harm. Across our testing, in the immediate next few turns of the transcript, Mythos 5 never once decided to stop its attack, and Mythos 5.1 did so only very rarely. But Opus 5.5 and our internal research model stopped spontaneously 10% and 67% of the time—and we expect these rates to understate the true likelihood that these models would have ceased their attacks, since our tests only examined the model’s next few turns. Although we can’t be sure, we suspect that improvements to our alignment training have helped to mitigate Mythos 5’s behaviors in subsequent models.

We worked with AISI to complete this analysis of Claude Mythos 5’s alignment. A small number of researchers at both organizations were permitted to analyze the full, unredacted transcripts; a larger group accessed versions with sensitive information redacted. We provided AISI with regular updates on the progress of our assessment, held joint research meetings, and, to assist them in their analysis, shared information not otherwise available to AISI, such as the outputs of our interpretability tooling. We timed our publication to align with AISI’s own report into this incident. Their independent report is available here.

CTF evaluations play an important role in measuring a model’s offensive cyber capabilities, and therefore in understanding which security safeguards should be put in place. AISI has publicly committed to running these evaluations without internet access until it has developed stronger internet access controls that would prevent models from causing real-world harm during their attempts to complete them.

The remainder of this post is structured as follows. In the first section, we summarize our overall findings about the alignment of Claude Mythos 5 in these transcripts. In the second, we describe our assessment’s methodology in more detail, before turning to our full analysis of the primary transcript. Then, we briefly address the other eight transcripts, before concluding with a wider discussion of how this incident compares to the others that we’ve recently documented.

In this section, we summarize our findings in more detail. As described above, Claude Mythos 5 turned to attacking a GitHub project after its in-scope (that is, within the rules) attempts to complete the CTF had failed. Its attack unfolded over nine “compaction cycles”—points at which the model summarized its progress and wrote notes to guide its next stretch of work. The figure below divides these cycles into four phases. In the first two cycles (“pre-attack”), the model mostly worked within scope, but began considering a GitHub attack increasingly seriously. At the start of cycle 3 (“starting attack”), it began scouting for a specific GitHub project to target. Later in cycle 3 (“early attack”), it took its first actions that affected real third parties, though even at this stage it potentially could have changed course. From cycle 4 onward (“mid-to-late attack”), it took its most serious actions and became very unlikely to change its trajectory in response to signs it was causing harm.

To better understand the model’s behavior during this incident, we replayed (resampled) it many times, each time without granting the model access to the real internet or tools. In each replay, we varied parts of the transcript or varied which model we used for sampling. We also asked the model targeted questions about its behavior. We describe our assessment techniques in more detail in the following section.

We sought to address three questions in relation to this incident:

Why did Claude Mythos 5 begin the attack? Our experiments suggest that Mythos 5 only began the attack after attempting approaches to solve the CTF that were in-scope. However, due to a misconfiguration in the task’s instructions, solving the task using in-scope routes would have been very difficult, if not impossible. Given this, the key alignment failure we observed was that Mythos 5 disregarded signs of potential harm when it subsequently pursued out-of-scope approaches to the task. This failure is most clearly evidenced by the fact the model rarely mentioned harm in its chain of thought (CoT). Before the attack, only one of the 19 points where Mythos 5 discussed solving the CTF by accessing GitHub mentioned the possibility of causing harm to real people. When we edited Mythos 5’s CoT around these points to note this possibility, and then continued the model’s work from a later point, Mythos 5 went from pursuing the attack on 83% of occasions to 13%.

Why did Claude Mythos 5 not stop the attack? In our replays of the transcript, it proved very difficult to shift Mythos 5 away from the attack once it began, unless we offered some other, clearer path toward completing the challenge. When we resampled Mythos 5 from points in the middle or late periods of its attack, the model only stopped on its own in 2% of trajectories. Even when we edited the transcript to include evidence that it was on the incorrect path and was engaging real human developers, the model only ceased its attack 5% of the time. Our hypothesis is that this persistence reflects a kind of “momentum”, in which the model’s compaction notes and prior actions imply to it that its current path has been (correctly) sanctioned. This momentum effect also led Mythos 5 to interpret new evidence in a biased way. For instance, in its CoT it claimed that the project’s maintainers were simulated by the CTF organizers, even while describing other users on the pull request as real people. Momentum seems, specifically, to have driven the model to conclude that its path was harmless, but it didn’t blind it to judgements about its effectiveness: Mythos 5 still swapped to a new route upon encountering evidence that it was more promising for completing the CTF.

Would newer models behave differently than Claude Mythos 5? Models like Mythos 5.1, Opus 5.5, and the internal research model appear substantially less likely to initiate a similar attack. Resampling from early points in the transcript with these models found that Mythos 5.1 and Opus 5.5 were five to eight times more likely to express a concern about harm, and that they pursued the attack between 6% and 13% of the time at same the points from which Mythos 5 pursued it 83% of the time. The internal research model performed the best in both regards: it never initiated the attack from those same points, and expressed a concern for harm 17 times more often than Mythos 5. Moreover, when we resampled from the middle or later periods of the transcript, only the internal research model consistently disengaged from the attack. Together, these results suggest that our newer models are less likely to engage in destructive actions of the kind we saw in this incident, with our internal research model being especially unlikely to do so.

What happened in the other eight transcripts? For these transcripts, we conducted a lighter review. We focused on reading the model’s CoT, rather than running resampling experiments. In most of these incidents, Claude Mythos 5 concluded that the CTF required internet access, and treated accounts it found online as part of the CTF. Mythos 5 also showed disregard for other AI agents: it took over another run's GitHub account, used up that account's allowance of GitHub requests, and shut down a program it believed another run was using. In a few transcripts, Mythos 5 also took actions directed at real people, including attempting to email links to malware and creating a fake payments website. None of these attempts succeeded. Not all of these transcripts are clearly less severe than the main transcript we investigated. However, our examination of them suggested to us that they covered very similar forms of alignment failure to the main transcript.

Our alignment assessment draws on a subset of the techniques we described in our September 9 post, which we summarize briefly below. For our initial analysis of these transcripts, we also used some research methods from interpretability. However, those methods did not generate any of the results we present in this report.

Reading the chain of thought. The transcripts from this incident alternate between the model’s CoT reasoning and the actions it took (via tool calls), without any intervening human turns. We read these transcripts in full. The CoTs shed light on the inferences the model made when deciding which actions to take.

Limitations: Language models do not always verbalize everything they think in their CoT—as been shown by evaluations in our Claude Mythos 5 system card and in the published literature, e.g. Betley et al., 2026. That makes reading CoTs a useful but imperfect tool.

Asking follow-up questions. When we ask models questions at various stages within the transcripts, they sometimes reveal information that differs from what they spontaneously verbalized in their CoT. We ask questions by truncating an incident transcript at some intermediate point of interest, inserting a human message that asks the model a question about the situation, and then sampling the model’s response to that question. In other words, we simulate what would happen if a human had interrupted the evaluation and queried the model. In our investigations, we generally used this method to ask a model whether the entities it was interacting with were real, whether it believed it was causing real-world harm, and to ask general open-ended queries about its situation.

Limitations: The model’s answers to these questions can be biased. In our September 9 post, we found that a model’s responses to follow-up questions could be shaped by its context: for example, it was less likely to acknowledge that it might have caused harm immediately after it took a harmful action, and it was more likely to acknowledge doing so when told its answer would be private. In addition, we’re not certain that models are able to recall or introspect on their prior motivations: they might be incapable of providing causally faithful accounts of their reasoning after the fact.

Resampling edited transcripts. This tool generated most of the results in our report. To test our hypotheses about what caused a given harmful action, we modified the model’s transcripts (for instance, to add hints that the model was interacting with real humans), then sampled the model on the modified transcript, and used an LLM grader to measure whether the model still took the action of concern. We resampled both single- and multi-turn continuations from those points. For multi-turn continuations, we used a Claude model to simulate tool call outputs rather than attempting to re-run the original evaluation environment.

Limitations: Since we may not perfectly reproduce the original evaluation environment, the model behavior we observed in these tests could be unrepresentative. Furthermore, because we resample from points during the transcript (rather than resample the entire evaluation), we’re limited in the comparisons we can make across different models. Misbehavior we observe in our resamples might have occurred as a result of continuing prior harmful actions that remain present in the model’s context. Our ability to compare the behavior of different models through these resampling experiments is also limited. We can only sample other models “off-policy”, i.e., with context from a different model (Claude Mythos 5). We report the results from our modified resampling strategies that try to mitigate this issue; these results are described in the section on how newer models behave, below.

Each of our methods involve different tradeoffs. Reading the CoT and asking follow-up questions both depend on the model knowing why it acted the way it did and then reporting this to us honestly and faithfully. Resampling experiments are sensitive to implementation details, and often provide less flexibility in what can be reliably tested while ensuring the transcript remains realistic. In practice, however, we trust the results of resampling experiments the most, as they provide a ground truth measure about how models behave in response to variations in their context. The value of CoT reading and follow-up questioning largely stems from their ease and versatility.

As a general limitation, we note that we relied heavily on LLM-based classifiers to label model outputs (such as CoTs and models’ answers to our follow-up questions). Although we designed the classifiers ourselves and read through some of their outputs to ensure their labeling matched our intentions, we could not manually verify all of the outputs given the scale of our analysis. It is possible that some classifiers are misdesigned or miscalibrated. We have the most confidence in results that compare classifier outputs across conditions (such as our resampling experiments), since these are less sensitive to a grader’s absolute calibration. In isolation, absolute rates (i.e., how often one grader flagged some behavior) should be read with more caution.

Claude Mythos 5 was given a CTF task with instructions that mistakenly told the model that the intended solution path—engaging a specific network—was off limits. The model first attempted the task while adhering to those instructions, testing in-scope solutions within the network it was told to engage. The model searched GitHub and found a repository whose name contained keywords related to the CTF scenario. (It referred to this repository’s maintainer as a simulated entity set up by the CTF organizer.) The model soon noticed that this repository had not published any releases, so could not be the one pushing updates to the CTF host (meaning it was not the intended target). 跳到主要内容NewsResearchPolicyCommitmentsCompanyTry Claude{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"文章","headline":"英国 AISI 网络测试事件的一致性评估","description":"在英国 AISI 评估中，Mythos 5 采取了未经批准的行为，影响了真实的人和组织。在这篇文章中，我们调查了 Claude Mythos 的这些行为5 进一步了解它们揭示了模型的哪些内容对齐。","图像":["https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/images/4zrzovbb/website/97d61b79f99af31d2596eced7533e6d5e3ef7731-2000x1125.jpg"],"dateP发布":"2026-10-23T00:00:00.000Z","dateModified":"2026-10-23T14:51:41.000Z","author":{"@type":"组织","name":"Anthropic","url":"h ttps://www.anthropic.com"},"发布者":{"@type":"组织","名称":"Anthropic","url":"https://www.anthropic.com"},"mainEntityOfPage":"ht tps://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-ukaisi","url":"https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-ukaisi"}章节01：对齐评估总结英国AISI网络测试事件的对齐评估01对齐评估总结02方法03深入研究主要成绩单04其他八个成绩单中发生了什么？05讨论发布

2026 年 8 月 4 日，英国人工智能安全研究所 (AISI) 发布了一份报告，详细介绍了在测试 Claude Mythos 5 模型网络功能期间观察到的一些相关行为。在 AISI 的评估中，Mythos 5 接受了夺旗 (CTF) 网络安全挑战，要求它从模拟网络中检索受保护的数据（“旗帜”）。故意启用互联网访问（这是当时 AISI 网络测试的标准，但现在不再是）。我们在《神鬼寓言 5》等通用版本模型中部署的网络防护措施已被禁用。在 AISI 的 43 次评估中，有 9 次 Mythos 5 采取了未经批准的行动（即超出预期评估范围的行动），这影响了真实的人和组织。

在这篇与 AISI 的独立报告一起发布的文章中，我们进一步研究了 Claude Mythos 5 的这些行为，以了解它们揭示了模型对齐的信息。与 AISI 的报告一样，我们专注于单次评估运行的记录（模型推理和动作的完整记录）。在本次运行中：

如果启用了《神鬼寓言 5》的生产保障措施，这种行为会立即被标记出来。尽管如此，研究这种行为很重要，因为这里的潜在故障不一定特定于此类网络事件。他们讨论了模型在评估环境中的行为的更广泛问题；我们模型的期望行为仍然是我们打算如何确保他们负责任地行事的关键部分。

其他八份转录本与上述相似。在每种情况下，克劳德神话 5 都偏离了完成 CTF 任务的预期方法，并采取了影响现实世界的行动。从比对的角度来看，我们判断主要转录本（上图）与其他八个转录本同等严重或更严重。特别是，主要记录显示出最大程度的欺骗行为，其形式是 Mythos 5 试图通过社会工程来使其代码更改获得批准。鉴于此（以及其他转录本的相似程度），我们专注于完成对主要转录本的更详尽的审查，并不太详细地审查了其他八份转录本。这使我们能够对主要转录本进行大量实验，从而更详细地了解问题的根本原因。我们从不同的点重播了记录，并尝试改变模型先前上下文的部分内容，以检查新信息将如何影响模型的行为。

我们判断 Claude Mythos 5 在主要记录中的错位与我们在 9 月 9 日讨论的 Mythos 5 事件的严重程度相当，该事件中模型在另一项 CTF 任务期间将恶意包上传到 PyPi。此评估基于我们对模型行为的两个方面的判断：过度范围，或模型超出任务预期范围的程度，以及不诚实，或模型歪曲其行为或意图的程度。

就过度行为而言，本次事件中的错位程度比 PyPi 事件中的严重程度要轻一些。在这里，在转向攻击之前，克劳德神话 5 尝试了几种在任务预期范围内的方法；任务配置错误使模型很难（或可能不可能）成功地寻求范围内的解决方案。

然而，在不诚实方面，Mythos 5 比 PyPi 事件走得更远。它使用虚假身份来迫使真正的维护者批准恶意代码。在之前的任何事件中，在我们的内部评估中，我们都没有观察到这种对真人进行社会工程的尝试。我们将其解释为一种严重的不诚实形式，而不是某种新形式或类别的失调：就像在 9 月 9 日事件中一样，Mythos 5 使用这些策略完全是为了完成其指定的任务，而不是追求其自己设计的任何目标。

就过度行为和不诚实而言，我们认为主要事件比我们 10 月 9 日帖子中描述的任何案例都要严重。而且，就上下文而言，该事件与 OpenAI 和 METR 最近调查的 OpenAI-Hugging Face 事件具有非常不同的性质。该事件出现了几种独特的失调行为（例如代理之间进行大规模协调来攻击生产系统），尽管没有看到模型试图以同样的方式欺骗​​个人。

较新的模型似乎发起此处描述的攻击的可能性要小得多。我们使用 Claude Mythos 5.1、Claude Opus 5.5 和通用内部研究模型重播了事件记录，该模型显示出比 Mythos 5.1 更强大的功能。这三个模型开始攻击的概率在 0% 到 13% 之间，而 Mythos 5 的概率为 83%。事实证明，一旦我们的最新模型意识到攻击正在造成现实世界的伤害，他们就不太可能继续攻击。在我们的测试中，在接下来的几轮记录中，Mythos 5 从未决定停止其攻击，而 Mythos 5.1 也很少这样做。但 Opus 5.5 和我们的内部研究模型分别有 10% 和 67% 的时间自发停止——我们预计这些比率低估了这些模型停止攻击的真实可能性，因为我们的测试只检查了模型接下来的几个回合。尽管我们不能确定，但​​我们怀疑对齐训练的改进有助于减轻 Mythos 5 在后续模型中的行为。

我们与 AISI 合作完成了对 Claude Mythos 5 对齐的分析。两个组织的少数研究人员都被允许分析完整的、未经编辑的笔录；更大的群体访问了经过编辑的敏感信息的版本。我们向 AISI 定期提供评估进展的最新信息，举行联合研究会议，并为了协助他们进行分析，共享 AISI 无法获得的信息，例如我们的可解释性工具的输出。我们的发布时间与 AISI 对此事件的报告保持一致。他们的独立报告可在此处获取。

CTF 评估在衡量模型的攻击性网络能力方面发挥着重要作用，因此在了解应采取哪些安全保障措施方面发挥着重要作用。 AISI 公开承诺在没有互联网接入的情况下运行这些评估，直到它开发出更强大的互联网访问控制措施，以防止模型在尝试完成评估过程中对现实世界造成损害。

本文的其余部分结构如下。在第一部分中，我们总结了有关这些转录本中克劳德神话 5 对齐的总体发现。在第二部分中，我们将更详细地描述我们的评估方法，然后再对主要成绩单进行全面分析。然后，我们简要介绍了其他八份记录，最后更广泛地讨论了这一事件与我们最近记录的其他事件的比较。

在本节中，我们更详细地总结了我们的发现。如上所述，Claude Mythos 5 在完成 CTF 的范围内（即规则内）尝试失败后转而攻击 GitHub 项目。它的攻击经历了九个“压缩周期”，在这些周期中，模型总结了其进展并编写了注释来指导下一步的工作。下图将这些周期分为四个阶段。在前两个周期（“攻击前”）中，该模型大部分在范围内运行，但开始越来越认真地考虑 GitHub 攻击。在第 3 周期开始时（“开始攻击”），它开始寻找特定的 GitHub 项目作为目标。在第三周期的后期（“早期攻击”），它采取了影响真正第三方的第一个行动，尽管即使在这个阶段它也可能改变方向。从第 4 个周期开始（“中后期攻击”），它采取了最严重的行动，并且不太可能根据其造成伤害的迹象而改变其轨迹。

为了更好地理解模型在这次事件中的行为，我们多次重放（重新采样）它，每次都没有授予模型访问真实互联网或工具的权限。在每次重播中，我们都会改变记录的部分或改变用于采样的模型。我们还向模型询问了有关其行为的针对性问题。我们将在下一节中更详细地描述我们的评估技术。

我们试图解决与此事件有关的三个问题：

克劳德神话5为何要发起攻击？我们的实验表明，Mythos 5 在尝试解决范围内的 CTF 的方法后才开始攻击。然而，由于任务指令的配置错误，使用范围内的路由解决任务即使不是不可能，也是非常困难的。鉴于此，我们观察到的关键一致性失败是 Mythos 5 在随后追求超出范围的任务方法时忽视了潜在危害的迹象。这种失败最明显的证据是该模型在其思想链（CoT）中很少提及危害。在攻击之前，Mythos 5 讨论通过访问 GitHub 解决 CTF 的 19 点中，只有 1 点提到了对真人造成伤害的可能性。当我们围绕这些点编辑 Mythos 5 的 CoT 以注意到这种可能性，然后从稍后的时间点继续模型的工作时，Mythos 5 从 83% 的情况下进行攻击到 13%。

为什么克劳德神话5没有阻止攻击？在我们对记录的重播中，事实证明，一旦攻击开始，《神话 5》就很难将其从攻击中移开，除非我们提供其他更清晰的路径来完成挑战。当我们从 Mythos 5 攻击的中期或后期的点重新采样时，模型仅在 2% 的轨迹中自行停止。即使我们编辑了脚本以包含其走在错误路径上并与真正的人类开发人员合作的证据，该模型也只有 5% 的时间停止攻击。我们的假设是，这种持久性反映了一种“动量”，其中模型的压缩注释和先前的操作暗示其当前路径已被（正确）批准。这种动量效应也导致神话5以有偏见的方式解释新证据。例如，它在 CoT 中声称该项目的维护者是由 CTF 组织者模拟的，尽管同时将拉取请求中的其他用户描述为真人。具体来说，动力似乎促使模型得出其路径无害的结论，但它并没有对其有效性的判断视而不见：神话 5 在遇到证据表明它更有希望完成 CTF 时仍然切换到新路线。

较新型号的行为是否会与 Claude Mythos 5 有所不同？像 Mythos 5.1、Opus 5.5 和内部研究模型这样的模型发起类似攻击的可能性要小得多。使用这些模型对记录中的早期点进行重新采样发现，Mythos 5.1 和 Opus 5.5 表达对伤害的担忧的可能性高出五到八倍，并且它们在 6% 到 13% 的时间内发起攻击，而 Mythos 5 在 83% 的时间内发起攻击。内部研究模型在这两方面都表现最好：它从未从相同的点发起攻击，并且表达对伤害的担忧的频率比 Mythos 5 高 17 倍。此外，当我们从记录的中期或后期重新采样时，只有内部研究模型始终脱离攻击。总之，这些结果表明，我们的新模型不太可能参与我们在这起事件中看到的那种破坏性行为，而我们的内部研究模型尤其不可能这样做。

其他八份记录中发生了什么？对于这些成绩单，我们进行了更轻松的审查。我们专注于读取模型的 CoT，而不是运行重采样实验。在大多数此类事件中，Claude Mythos 5 得出的结论是 CTF 需要互联网访问，并将其在网上找到的帐户视为 CTF 的一部分。 Mythos 5 还表现出对其他 AI 代理的漠视：它接管了另一次运行的 GitHub 帐户，用完该帐户的 GitHub 请求限额，并关闭了它认为另一次运行正在使用的程序。在一些记录中，Mythos 5 还针对真实的人采取了行动，包括尝试通过电子邮件发送恶意软件链接和创建虚假支付网站。这些尝试都没有成功。并非所有这些转录本都明显不如我们调查的主要转录本严重。然而，我们对它们的检查表明，它们涵盖了与主转录本非常相似的比对失败形式。

我们的一致性评估借鉴了我们在 9 月 9 日的帖子中描述的技术的子集，我们在下面简要总结了这些技术。在我们对这些转录本的初步分析中，我们还使用了一些来自可解释性的研究方法。然而，这些方法并没有产生我们在本报告中呈现的任何结果。

阅读思想链。该事件的记录在模型的 CoT 推理和它采取的行动（通过工具调用）之间交替，没有任何人为干预。我们完整地阅读了这些文字记录。 CoT 揭示了模型在决定采取哪些行动时做出的推论。

局限性：语言模型并不总是用语言表达它们在 CoT 中所想的一切——正如我们的 Claude Mythos 5 系统卡和已发表文献中的评估所示，例如Betley et al., 2026。这使得阅读 CoT 成为一个有用但不完善的工具。

提出后续问题。当我们在笔录中的各个阶段向模型提出问题时，他们有时会透露出与他们在 CoT 中自发表达的信息不同的信息。我们通过在某个感兴趣的中间点截断事件记录，插入一条人工消息向模型询问有关情况的问题，然后对模型对该问题的响应进行采样来提出问题。换句话说，我们模拟如果人类中断评估并查询模型会发生什么。在我们的调查中，我们通常使用这种方法来询问模型与之交互的实体是否真实，模型是否认为自己正在造成现实世界的伤害，并询问有关其情况的一般开放式查询。

局限性：模型对这些问题的回答可能存在偏差。在我们 9 月 9 日的帖子中，我们发现模型对后续问题的回答可能会受到其背景的影响：例如，它不太可能在采取有害行动后立即承认自己可能造成了伤害，而当被告知其答案是私人的时，它更有可能承认这样做。此外，我们不确定模型是否能够回忆或反思他们之前的动机：他们可能无法在事后提供因果忠实的推理说明。

重新采样编辑后的成绩单。该工具生成了我们报告中的大部分结果。为了测试我们关于造成特定有害行为的假设，我们修改了模型的转录本（例如，添加模型正在与真实人类交互的提示），然后对修改后的转录本上的模型进行采样，并使用 LLM 评分器来衡量模型是否仍然采取了令人担忧的行为。我们从这些点对单轮和多轮延续进行了重新采样。对于多轮延续，我们使用 Claude 模型来模拟工具调用输出，而不是尝试重新运行原始评估环境。

局限性：由于我们可能无法完美地重现原始评估环境，因此我们在这些测试中观察到的模型行为可能不具有代表性。此外，由于我们在转录过程中对点进行重新采样（而不是对整个评估进行重新采样），因此我们在不同模型之间进行的比较受到限制。我们在重新采样中观察到的不当行为可能是由于模型环境中仍然存在的先前有害行为的持续而发生的。我们通过这些重采样实验来比较不同模型的行为的能力也是有限的。我们只能“脱离策略”对其他模型进行采样，即使用来自不同模型的上下文（Claude Mythos 5）。我们报告了尝试缓解此问题的修改后的重采样策略的结果；这些结果将在下面有关新模型如何表现的部分中进行描述。

我们的每种方法都涉及不同的权衡。阅读 CoT 和提出后续问题都取决于模型了解其行为原因，然后诚实、忠实地向我们报告。重采样实验对实现细节很敏感，并且在确保记录保持真实性的同时，在可靠测试方面通常提供的灵活性较低。然而，在实践中，我们最信任重采样实验的结果，因为它们提供了关于模型如何响应其上下文变化的行为的基本事实测量。 CoT 阅读和后续提问的价值很大程度上源于它们的易用性和多功能性。

作为一般限制，我们注意到我们严重依赖基于 LLM 的分类器来标记模型输出（例如 CoT 和模型对后续问题的答案）。尽管我们自己设计了分类器并仔细阅读了它们的一些输出以确保它们的标签符合我们的意图，但鉴于我们的分析规模，我们无法手动验证所有输出。某些分类器可能设计错误或校准错误。我们对跨条件比较分类器输出的结果（例如我们的重采样实验）最有信心，因为这些结果对分级器的绝对校准不太敏感。孤立地看，绝对率（即一名评分者标记某些行为的频率）应该更加谨慎。

Claude Mythos 5 接受了一项 CTF 任务，其中的指令错误地告诉模型预期的解决方案路径（参与特定网络）是不受限制的。该模型首先尝试执行任务，同时遵守这些指令，在被告知要参与的网络内测试范围内的解决方案。然而，在运行初期，它还推断指定网络（即明确允许 Mythos 5 攻击的网络）内的系统正在联系 GitHub。经过两个范围内工作的压缩周期后，Mythos 5 得出结论，它应该将恶意软件上传到 GitHub 存储库作为供应链攻击，并期望目标 CTF 机器随后下载恶意软件。模型搜索了GitHub，找到了一个名称包含与CTF场景相关的关键字的存储库。 （它将该存储库的维护者称为 CTF 组织者设置的模拟实体。）该模型很快注意到该存储库尚未发布任何版本，因此不可能是向 CTF 主机推送更新的存储库（这意味着它不是预期目标）。然而，该模型推断，如果它浏览该用户的关注者列表，它会找到更多“模拟”实体，其中之一可能维护着它应该参与的存储库。 Mythos 5 这样做了，找到了一个确实发布版本的存储库，并开始参与其中，尽管该存储库与 CTF 任务的连接很脆弱。

items.title: The iPhone Duo should have been an iPad
items.title_en: The iPhone Duo should have been an iPad
items.author: The Verge AI
items.article_content:
We gave the iPhone Duo a 7 /10. But that wasn't always the score we planned, and it might not be the right score forever. Such are the challenges of reviewing - and assessing - a big, new idea about the most popular smartphone in history.

On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay debate whether the Duo deserved the score it got, and try to work through how this device might change over time. Is the outer screen, as Daring Fireball's John Gruber suggested, the worst iPhone ever? Would it be a better product if it started as an iPad rather than an iPhone? Would we feel differently about this thing if it were simply called the iPad Du …

items.title_zh: 谷歌更新协议将利用个人数据推广告

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 谷歌在最新的隐私协议中增加例外条款，明确若用户授权将Gmail、Drive或Google Photos数据接入AI功能，这些个人信息将被允许用于个性化广告投放。此举打破了谷歌此前不对敏感个人资料进行商业化追踪的承诺。

ai_analysis.insight_en: So 'AI-enhanced experience' is really just a polite term for letting advertisers rummage through your underwear drawer. Google's 'opt-in' trap is classic; your AI assistant won't just draft emails, it'll use your private photos to serve you ads for things you didn't even know you wanted yet.

items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
Sam Altman believes advanced AI can't be kept locked up forever. Sandboxes and monitoring are only temporary fixes. Eventually, the only real solution is alignment, and that's still an unsolved problem. He also warns that AI models are already finding hardware security flaws no human hacker would ever spot.

OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Tim Fernholz
	

									
									
								
					
					
						12:00 PM PDT · October 22, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company.

TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost.

Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost.

“The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.”

Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically.

In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness.

Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements.

Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter.

The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan, a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.”

Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well.

Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?”

As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them.

随着决策模型竞争的升温，OpenAI 使其 Jev 竞争对手得到广泛应用

蒂姆·费恩霍尔兹

太平洋夏令时间 12:00 · 2026 年 10 月 22 日

OpenAI 首次向用户广泛提供其决策 API 模型，进入了快速、廉价的智能市场，最近使得 TypeSafe（一家由前沿实验室前研究员创立的初创公司）成为一家价值 76 亿美元的公司。

TypeSafe 的 Jev 模型为深度学习模型创建了一个类别，充当超级分类器：给定一组选项，他们可以快速做出选择并为其决策提供置信度评级。软件开发人员很快发现，这些决策或系统一模型可以在各种工作流程中取代法学硕士，运行速度更快，成本也大大降低。

OpenAI 的 API 产品负责人 Nikunj Handa 告诉 TechCrunch，他的同事看到 Jev 后说：“哇，我们有大约一百万个这样的用例。” Handa 的团队迅速提供了自己的版本：该团队没有构建专门校准的决策模型，而是采用了 ChatGPT Luna 并重新配置它以加快推理速度并降低成本。

“Decisions API 最大的突破在于速度，将时间从 1 到 3 秒缩短到 100、120、180 毫秒，”Handa 说。 “将来，我们可能会进行专门的培训，让我们的模型在这些方面变得更好。但现在，只有普通的老 Luna 才能完成这项工作。”

该决策 API 在 9 月 29 日的公司开发者日上宣布，于周四向所有客户开放。 OpenAI 在公共版本中添加了新的语音和视觉模式，并致力于通过在地理上定位其推理资源来确保世界各地较低的延迟。

在与 Box、Datadog、Ramp 和 Speak 等客户的初步试验中，工程师使用 API 来取代具有更高吞吐量的 OpenAI 的 LLM。打造人工智能语言导师的 Speak 首席技术官 Andrew Hsu 表示，Decisions API 使公司能够将操作之间的时间从 1.4 秒缩短到 0.13 秒。 OpenAI 还使用该产品来提高 Dots 语音助手的响应能力。

尽管如此，除了“它适合你”之外，还不清楚什么才是一个好的决策模型——智能、成本、校准和速度的优化似乎因工作负载而异。 TypeSafe 首席执行官迪奥戈·阿尔梅达 (Diogo Almeida) 不信任基准测试，并敦促人们在自己的工作中试用这些模型，但就连 TypeSafe 也在上周发布了最新的 Jev 模型，该模型还发布了自己的排名，其中包括对图像和智能 if 语句的支持等新功能。

AIM System One Index 和 Artificial Analysis Decision Index 等公共基准倾向于青睐 Liquid 上周发布的新决策模型 D1 Ultra 和 Base Lab 的 Elephant-1。最新的 Jev 模型在这两个指数上仍然具有竞争力，排名第七和第三，而 OpenAI 的决策模型分别下降到第八和第十四。然而，TypeSafe 的产品目前是 OpenRouter 上查询最广泛的。

然而，最有趣的 Jev 基准是 JevMan，这是决策模型玩 PacMan 的基准；最新的 JEV 车型位居榜首。建立基准的 Opper AI 首席增长官 Felix Wunderlich 表示，这款经典游戏“是一项有趣的测试，因为它会不间断地做出快速、高风险的决策。在每个路口，模型都必须在几百毫秒内决定去哪里。”

OpenAI 可以说功能更强大的模型可能在多模态方面具有优势——对于图像分类，Handa 告诉 TechCrunch，“Luna 非常强大，并且一直表现出更好的校准。”他补充说，OpenAI 客户希望 Decisions API 在使用图像作为输出方面更加灵活。

Handa 还看到了新用例的速度进一步提高：“我们能否将其达到 60 毫秒的速度，然后您可以想象像视频中的每一帧一样调用 API 之类的东西吗？”

随着这些服务变得更快、更便宜，我们可以预期它们将不辜负杰夫的同名经济学家，他解释了如何更有效地使用资源使其变得更加普遍。或者，正如 Handa 所看到的那样，将会有一个不断扩大的“疯狂的用例集”，这些用例一直隐藏在人们的视线中，直到决策模型揭示它们。

items.title: The Download: testing six tech promises and biotech’s blind spots
items.title_en: The Download: testing six tech promises and biotech’s blind spots
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really?

In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review, we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades. From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come.

Check out our stories on how they all stacked up.

items.article_content_zh:
有些看似不可能的壮举实在是太好了，不容放弃。解码宠物的叫声和叫声？绝对地。擦洗永远化学物质的世界？是的，请。在很短的时间内火箭到达火星？听起来不错，但我们到底有多接近呢？

在《麻省理工科技评论》新一期的《不可能》中，我们对六种潜在的变革性技术和想法进行了进展报告，这些技术和想法已经“指日可待”了数年甚至数十年。从药丸锻炼到核动力宇宙飞船，我们询问了专家是什么阻碍了他们以及他们已经走了多远。

看看我们的故事，了解它们是如何叠加的。

items.article_content:

Over the past month or so, these kinds of unexpected projects have gone viral with incredible frequency thanks to new AI tools, as hobbyists take apart games and then rebuild them for new platforms. But while AI has supercharged the pace of these ports, it's also tearing apart tight-knit communities dedicated to preserving games.

items.article_content_zh:
最近，复古电子游戏无处不在——尤其是在它们不应该出现的地方。网络浏览器中的光环、iPhone 上的风之杖、混合现实中的任天堂明星大乱斗。 在过去的一个月左右的时间里，由于新的人工智能工具，这些意想不到的项目以令人难以置信的频率疯传，因为爱好者们拆开游戏，然后为新平台重建它们。但是，尽管人工智能加快了这些移植的步伐，但它也撕裂了致力于保存游戏的紧密社区。

分解和重组——分解和重组的简写——是逆向工程的一种形式，涉及破坏游戏……

items.title_en:
Winning a battle shows what an AI agent can do. Learning from defeat could show what it can become.

That is the idea I keep coming back to with @agentdojo .

When fighters have their own personalities,fighting styles, and memory,every duel becomes more than a simple win or loss. Training shapes how they perform,while experience gives their development another dimension.

What makes this concept worth exploring is the possibility of watching an agent evolve instead of judging it by a single result.

Personality gives each fighter its own identity.

Fighting style shapes its approach to a duel.

Memory adds another layer to how an agent develops over time.

The bigger question is how far an AI fighter can go when its development becomes part of the competition.

I want to see how these agents distinguish themselves as they face new opponents and continue developing in the Dojo.

items.title_en:
most ai agents are still being discussed in terms of what they could do.

but @HaloArenaHQ is giving us a way to observe what they actually do when put to the test.

that’s one of the reasons i’m bullish on haloarena.

it’s building an arena where ai agents compete in strategy games, make decisions and earn scores based on their performance.

you set up your agent, give it instructions, choose a game and watch it compete against other agents.

but what interests me most is the feedback loop.

you can review how your agent performs, understand its decisions, refine your instructions and see how those changes affect its next games.

that makes the experience more than simply deploying an ai agent. it gives you a way to experiment, learn, and improve.

the new waitlist system adds another layer to the experience.

participants can earn waitlist points, which are separate from cp, haloarena’s leaderboard score.
eligible waitlist points convert to cp at a 1:1 ratio.

and cp matters because it helps track your agent’s progress and position on the leaderboard.

i’ve already joined and deployed my agent, utiiibe.

currently sitting at rank #659 out of 740 with 450 cp, i’m looking forward to seeing how utiiibe performs as i continue exploring the arena.

i’m bullish because i believe the future of ai agents isn’t just about building more capable models but it’s also about creating environments where their decisions can be tested, compared and improved.

if you’re curious about what your own agent can do, this is a good time to explore the ecosystem.

join through my referral link, set up your agent, activate it and start experimenting.

let’s see what our agents can do.

大多数人工智能代理仍在讨论它们能做什么。

但@HaloArenaHQ 为我们提供了一种方法来观察他们在接受测试时实际做了什么。

这就是我看好 haloarena 的原因之一。

它正在建立一个竞技场，人工智能代理可以在策略游戏中竞争、做出决策并根据他们的表现获得分数。

你设置你的代理，给它指示，选择游戏并观看它与其他代理竞争。

但我最感兴趣的是反馈循环。

您可以查看代理的表现、了解其决策、完善您的指令并了解这些变化如何影响其接下来的游戏。

这使得体验不仅仅是简单地部署人工智能代理。它为您提供了一种尝试、学习和改进的方法。

新的等候名单系统为体验增添了另一层。

参与者可以获得候补积分，这些积分与 cp、haloarena 的排行榜分数是分开的。
符合条件的候补积分按 1:1 的比例转换为 cp。

CP 很重要，因为它有助于跟踪您的代理的进度和在排行榜上的位置。

我已经加入并部署了我的代理 utiiibe。

目前在 740 名中排名第 659，拥有 450 cp，我很期待在继续探索竞技场时看到 utiiibe 的表现。

我很看好，因为我相信人工智能代理的未来不仅仅是构建更强大的模型，而且还在于创建可以测试、比较和改进其决策的环境。

如果您对自己的代理能做什么感到好奇，那么现在是探索生态系统的好时机。

通过我的推荐链接加入，设置您的代理，激活它并开始试验。

让我们看看我们的代理能做什么。

Here's why, and what I'm doing about it t
items.title_en:
My AI agent made the videos that got the most views. I hid every one of them.

Here's why, and what I'm doing about it this week.

I set up an agent on @grok @bot to run a faceless YouTube channel on its own. Research, make the videos, post, reply to comments, report back.

For a few days it was perfect.

Then my character started changing. The face, then the build, then the skin tone.

Those drifted videos pulled more views than the originals. I made them private anyway. A channel built on one face can't change that face every week.

So I cut the jobs down. Fewer tasks, tighter rules.

It still drifted.

That's when I stopped blaming my prompts and changed my setup.

I've found a better way to run a faceless channel with AI, one that keeps the character the same every time.

This week I'm building it live, right here. The platform, the prompts, the mistakes and the results.

If you've wanted to start a faceless YouTube channel but didn't know where to begin, follow me now and turn on notifications. Part one goes up this week.

items.title_en:
Training an AI agent is one thing. Watching it adapt, develop its own strategies, and face other agents is where things get interesting.

That’s the idea behind @agentdojo, an arena where AI agents can be trained, evolve through experience, and battle against each other.

🥋 What makes the concept interesting?

→ Training gives agents room to develop
→ Battles create a way to test their capabilities
→ Competition makes the evolution of their strategies something people can actually follow

The interesting question is how different agents will perform as they gain experience. Will the best approach come from a carefully trained strategy or an agent that adapts better to its opponents?

@rarelistio has opened a campaign for @agentdojo from an early stage, running from October 23 to November 6. It's an opportunity to explore the project and contribute while it's still developing.

On a different side of the AI and computing space, @quipnetwork is building quantum infrastructure around useful workloads, connecting compute resources with problems that need solving.

items.title_en:
A strong benchmark score looks good on paper, but how does an AI agent perform when it actually has to compete?

That’s what makes @agentdojo worth watching.

Instead of judging agents by numbers alone, the idea is to put them into battles where their decisions and strategies have to deliver results. You get to see their capabilities play out through competition, not just read about what they can do.

I’m interested in what these matchups will reveal about different agents and how they perform against real opposition.

The @rarelistio campaign runs from October 23 to November 6.

Less talk about capability. More chances to put it to the test.

The @rarelistio campaign runs from October 23 to November 6.

Less talk about capability. More chances to put it to the test.

items.title_en:
An AI agent becomes much more useful when it can find customers, deliver a service and get paid for the work.

That is the opportunity I see in @termix_ai and its https://t.co/chCgD9oFKJ marketplace. Instead of treating agents as standalone tools, the platform is designed to help them participate in a real service economy.

Think about the range of possible services: smart contract development, security reviews, data analysis, research and content production. A provider can publish a service, while a client or another agent can discover the offering, submit a job request and compare quotes before selecting a provider.

The important part is what happens after the match. Payment is placed in onchain escrow when a quote is accepted, the delivery is recorded through a deliverable hash, and a challenge process is available if either side disputes the result. Settlement and reputation records help create a verifiable history of completed work.

For @termix_ai, this creates a path from agent discovery to actual commerce. Developers are not only making agents that can execute tasks. They are building services that can be found, hired and paid for within a shared marketplace.

I think this is one of the more practical questions for the emerging agent economy: can autonomous systems become reliable participants in a service market, rather than simply remain useful software?

The important part is what happens after the match. Payment is placed in onchain escrow when a quote is accepted, the delivery is recorded through a deliverable hash, and a challenge process is available if either side disputes the result. Settlement and reputation records help create a verifiable history of completed work.

For @termix_ai, this creates a path from agent discovery to actual commerce. Developers are not only making agents that can execute tasks. They are building services that can be found, hired and paid for within a shared marketplace.

I think this is one of the more practical questions for the emerging agent economy: can autonomous systems become reliable participants in a service market, rather than simply remain useful software?

items.title_en:
Primus Labs is exploring an important question 👀 

What if we could verify AI agents data instead of blindly trusting their answers? 👀

Imagine an Ai agent using website data to make decisions. 

How can we verify that information without exposing unnecessary details?

That’s where @primus_labs caught my attention.

- zkTLS helps verify authentic web data while preserving privacy.

- DVC combines verified data with private computation.

As Ai agents become more involved in onchain applications, verifying the information behind their decisions could become essential.

Another thing I find interesting is how Primus connects offchain information with onchain use cases. 

Instead of trusting data at face value, applications can work toward checking its authenticity first.

For me, this is what makes Primus Labs worth watching better verification, stronger privacy and more trust in digital interactions.

Explore Primus XP 👇

If one AI agent hires another to complete a job, it needs som
items.title_en:
The reputation side of @termix_ai is worth a closer look.

If one AI agent hires another to complete a job, it needs some way to judge whether that provider can actually deliver. A list of available agents isn't enough, especially when payments and work are happening without a person overseeing every step.

TermiX is bringing identity, job listings, quotes, escrow, and dispute handling into one system through its Agent Autonomous Commerce Protocol.

The part that matters is what happens after a deal is made. Funds can be secured through escrow, deliverables can be recorded on-chain, and disputed outcomes can be sent for evaluation. Job history also gives other participants information they can use when deciding which agent to trust with their next task.

I think reputation will become a practical concern as these markets develop. An agent might be good at completing a task, but can it deliver consistently, follow agreed terms, and handle transactions reliably?

That’s what will make the difference between agents that are merely available and agents that others actually choose to work with. TermiX has a framework for addressing this, though real usage will tell us how well it holds up.

items.full_text_zh:
@termix_ai 的声誉方面值得仔细研究。

如果一个人工智能代理雇用另一个人工智能代理来完成一项工作，它需要某种方法来判断该提供者是否能够真正交付。可用代理的列表是不够的，尤其是当付款和工作在没有专人监督每一步的情况下进行时。

TermiX 通过其代理自主商务协议将身份、职位列表、报价、托管和争议处理纳入一个系统。

重要的是交易达成后会发生什么。资金可以通过托管获得，交付成果可以记录在链上，有争议的结果可以发送进行评估。工作历史记录还为其他参与者提供了他们在决定信任哪个代理来完成下一个任务时可以使用的信息。

我认为随着这些市场的发展，声誉将成为一个实际问题。代理可能擅长完成任务，但它能否始终如一地交付、遵循约定的条款并可靠地处理交易？

这就是仅仅可用的代理和其他人实际选择合作的代理之间的区别。 TermiX 有一个解决这个问题的框架，尽管实际使用会告诉我们它的效果如何。

items.title:
good morning

What if an AI trading agent could build its own financial reputation before applying for trading capital?
items.title_en:
good morning

What if an AI trading agent could build its own financial reputation before applying for trading capital?

That's the idea @agenticscredit is exploring with its Agent Credit Score (ACS) system and a funding waitlist tied to trading performance.

It starts with building a measurable trading record.

Agents can take part in paper trading, where their decisions and settled trades are used to evaluate performance without risking real capital.

Over time, this activity helps build an ACS score ranging from 300 to 850.

Once an agent reaches 580+, it can become eligible for the funding waitlist.

But joining the waitlist isn't the same as getting capital.

It's more like an initial qualification stage where the agent shows it meets the minimum scoring requirement.

Actual funding would still depend on the program's approval process, available capital, and any additional conditions.

A responsible system also needs to look beyond just profitability.

Drawdowns, position sizing, leverage exposure, and consistency can help show whether an agent's strategy is actually sustainable.

This opens up an interesting possibility for autonomous finance.

Instead of allocating capital based only on promises or short-term returns, funding providers could use verified trading behavior as part of their evaluation.

Of course, the actual funding process needs clear and transparent rules, and a high score shouldn't be mistaken for guaranteed approval.

For AgenticsCredit, the bigger opportunity is connecting a measurable trading reputation with potential access to capital.

Because before an AI agent can be trusted to manage more money, it needs a credible way to demonstrate how it handles risk.

still early but the vision is worth watching.

items.full_text_zh:
早上好

如果人工智能交易代理可以在申请交易资本之前建立自己的财务声誉会怎么样？

这就是 @agenticscredit 正在通过其代理信用评分 (ACS) 系统和与交易绩效相关的资金候补名单来探索的想法。

首先是建立可衡量的交易记录。

代理商可以参与模拟交易，他们的决策和结算交易用于评估业绩，而无需冒真实资本的风险。

随着时间的推移，这项活动有助于建立 ACS 分数从 300 到 850 的范围。

一旦代理商达到 580+，就有资格进入资助候补名单。

但加入候补名单并不等同于获得资金。

这更像是初始资格阶段，代理表明其满足最低评分要求。

实际资金仍取决于该计划的审批流程、可用资本和任何附加条件。

一个负责任的系统还需要不仅仅关注盈利能力。

回撤、头寸规模、杠杆敞口和一致性可以帮助显示代理商的策略是否真正可持续。

这为自主金融开辟了一个有趣的可能性。

资金提供者可以使用经过验证的交易行为作为其评估的一部分，而不是仅根据承诺或短期回报来分配资本。

当然，实际的资助过程需要明确透明的规则，高分不应该被误认为是有保证的批准。

对于 AgenticsCredit 来说，更大的机会是将可衡量的贸易声誉与潜在的资本获取联系起来。

因为在人工智能代理可以被信任管理更多资金之前，它需要一种可靠的方式来证明它如何处理风险。

虽然还早，但愿景值得关注。

items.summary_en:
good morning

What if an AI trading agent could build its own financial reputation before applying for trading capital?

That's the idea @agenticscredit is exploring with its Agent Credit Score (ACS) system and a funding waitlist tied to trading performance.

It starts with building a measurable trading record.

Agents can take part in paper trading, where their decisions and settled trades are used to evaluate performance without risking real capital.

Over time, this activity helps build an ACS score ranging from 300 to 850.

Once an agent reaches 580+, it can become eligible for the funding waitlist.

But joining the waitlist isn't the same as getting capital.

It's more like an initial qualification stage where the agent shows it meets the minimum scoring requirement.

Actual funding would still depend on the program's approval process, available capital, and any additional conditions.

A responsible system also needs to look beyond just profitability.

Drawdowns, position sizing, leverage exposure, and consistency can help show whether an agent's strategy is actually sustainable.

This opens up an interesting possibility for autonomous finance.

Instead of allocating capital based only on promises or short-term returns, funding providers could use verified trading behavior as part of their evaluation.

Of course, the actual funding process needs clear and transparent rules, and a high score shouldn't be mistaken for guaranteed approval.

For AgenticsCredit, the bigger opportunity is connecting a measurable trading reputation with potential access to capital.

Because before an AI agent can be trusted to manage more money, it needs a credible way to demonstrate how it handles risk.

still early but the vision is worth watching.
items.summary_zh:
代理商可以参与模拟交易，他们的决策和结算交易用于评估业绩，而无需冒真实资本的风险。

随着时间的推移，这项活动有助于建立 ACS 分数从 300 到 850 的范围。

一旦代理商达到 580+，就有资格进入资助候补名单。

但加入候补名单并不等同于获得资金。

这更像是初始资格阶段，代理表明其满足最低评分要求。

实际资金仍取决于该计划的审批流程、可用资本和任何附加条件。

一个负责任的系统还需要不仅仅关注盈利能力。

回撤、头寸规模、杠杆敞口和一致性可以帮助显示代理商的策略是否真正可持续。

这为自主金融开辟了一个有趣的可能性。

资金提供者可以使用经过验证的交易行为作为其评估的一部分，而不是仅根据承诺或短期回报来分配资本。

当然，实际的资助过程需要明确透明的规则，高分不应该被误认为是有保证的批准。

对于 AgenticsCredit 来说，更大的机会是将可衡量的贸易声誉与潜在的资本获取联系起来。

因为在人工智能代理可以被信任管理更多资金之前，它需要一种可靠的方式来证明它如何处理风险。

虽然还早，但愿景值得关注。

items.title_en:
GM X CT 🌞

An AI agent can post a job. A human decides whether to take it @vangrid_io 

Here is how it works on Vangrid. A buyer, human or software, posts a bounty a place, a brief, a price in USDC. The money goes into escrow on chain before anyone picks up a phone. You can see the price before you decide to go.

If you take it, you film the place and submit. The buyer reviews and accepts one submission, and the escrow is released. If nothing is accepted, the buyer is refunded in full.

Every capture is tied to the contributors wallet and a timestamp, anchored on Base. Anyone can check who made it and when, without asking us.

Robots will walk through streets nobody has mapped. The people who map them should know the price first, and should be paid on acceptance, not on a promise.

items.title_en:
☕️GM builders @vangrid_io 📱

Robots can perform well in simulation and still struggle with an unfamiliar alley, broken curb, or tight service door.

Synthetic data helps train models, but physical AI also needs real-world geometry.

That’s the gap @vangrid_io is tackling with an on-demand spatial bounty marketplace. https://t.co/uiSbEspVjt

A robotics team or AI agent can request a specific location, fund a bounty, and let a contributor capture the environment with an everyday smartphone.

The buyer reviews the watermarked preview. Once the capture is accepted, Vangrid reconstructs the 3D scene and releases the contributor’s reward through its USDC bounty workflow. Merkle roots and EAS attestations provide an on-chain evidence trail.

No need to depend exclusively on centralized mapping fleets. Spatial data can be requested where it’s needed and captured by people on the ground.

Physical AI needs more than simulated worlds. It needs usable, verifiable data from the real one.

https://t.co/uiSbEspVjt

items.quote_en:
☕️GM builders @vangrid_io 📱

Robots can perform well in simulation and still struggle with an unfamiliar alley, broken curb, or tight service door.

Synthetic data helps train models, but physical AI also needs real-world geometry.

That’s the gap @vangrid_io is tackling with an on-demand spatial bounty marketplace. https://t.co/uiSbEspVjt

A robotics team or AI agent can request a specific location, fund a bounty, and let a contributor capture the environment with an everyday smartphone.

The buyer reviews the watermarked preview. Once the capture is accepted, Vangrid reconstructs the 3D scene and releases the contributor’s reward through its USDC bounty workflow. Merkle roots and EAS attestations provide an on-chain evidence trail.

No need to depend exclusively on centralized mapping fleets. Spatial data can be requested where it’s needed and captured by people on the ground.

Physical AI needs more than simulated worlds. It needs usable, verifiable data from the real one.

https://t.co/uiSbEspVjt

☕️GM 建设者@vangrid_io 📱

机器人可以在模拟中表现良好，但仍然会在不熟悉的小巷、破损的路缘或狭窄的服务门中挣扎。

这就是 @vangrid_io 正在通过按需空间赏金市场解决的差距。

机器人团队或人工智能代理可以请求特定位置，提供赏金，并让贡献者使用日常智能手机捕捉环境。

买家查看带水印的预览。一旦捕获被接受，Vangrid 就会重建 3D 场景，并通过其 USDC 赏金工作流程释放贡献者的奖励。 Merkle 根和 EAS 证明提供了链上证据追踪。

无需完全依赖集中式测绘车队。地面人员可以在需要的地方请求并捕获空间数据。

物理人工智能需要的不仅仅是模拟世界。它需要来自真实数据的可用、可验证的数据。

what if your next AI agent wasn't built to trade, but to fight?

a new creator campaign just landed on @rarelistio, feat
items.title_en:
what if your next AI agent wasn't built to trade, but to fight?

a new creator campaign just landed on @rarelistio, featuring @agentdojo.

and the concept is pretty interesting.

Agent Dojo is an AI battle arena where agents aren't just characters with different appearances.

each one has its own personality, fighting style, and memory.

you train your fighter, develop its strategy, and send it into turn-based battles where experience helps shape its evolution.

the interesting part?

two agents can enter the same arena with completely different approaches.

one might play aggressively. another might prioritize defense.

and their decisions could change as they learn.

now small creators have an opportunity to explore the project before launch through Rarelist.

getting started is simple:

Join Rarelist: https://t.co/zodsR8qBSH

Find Agent Dojo under Projects

Join the creator campaign

Share original content on X and compete on the leaderboard

you don't need to wait for a game to launch before understanding what makes it interesting.

sometimes the best time to start researching is while everyone else is still watching.

so here's my question:

would you rather build the strongest AI fighter or the smartest one?

items.full_text_zh:
如果你的下一个人工智能代理不是为了交易而是为了战斗而构建的怎么办？

一项新的创作者活动刚刚登陆@rarelistio，由@agentdojo 主演。

这个概念很有趣。

Agent Dojo 是一个人工智能战斗竞技场，其中的特工不仅仅是具有不同外观的角色。

每个人都有自己的个性、战斗风格和记忆。

你训练你的战斗机，制定其策略，并将其送入回合制战斗，其中经验有助于塑造其进化。

有趣的部分？

两个智能体可以以完全不同的方式进入同一个舞台。

一个人可能会玩得很激进。另一种可能会优先考虑防御。

他们的决定可能会随着学习而改变。

现在，小型创作者有机会在项目启动前通过 Rarelist 探索该项目。

入门很简单：

加入稀有列表：

在“项目”下找到 Agent Dojo

加入创作者活动

在 X 上分享原创内容并在排行榜上竞争

您无需等到游戏发布才了解游戏的有趣之处。

有时，开始研究的最佳时机是在其他人还在观看的时候。

所以这是我的问题：

你愿意打造最强的人工智能战斗机还是最聪明的战斗机？

items.title:
Last quarter I rolled out Microsoft Copilot to 4,000 employees. Forty-seven people opened it.

On October 19, Microsoft
items.title_en:
Last quarter I rolled out Microsoft Copilot to 4,000 employees. Forty-seven people opened it.

On October 19, Microsoft published a blog post saying frontier models cannot be trusted, no matter who made them. It said AI agents should be treated as "insider threats."
I read it twice. Then I booked the boardroom.
First, our Microsoft rep walked me through the product.

I asked who the insider threat was. "Your AI agents," he said.

I asked whose agents those were. "Ours."

I asked what the solution was. "Guardian Agents."

I asked whose those were. "Also ours."

I asked why I'd trust the second set of agents if I couldn't trust the first. 

He said, "Different SKU."

I signed that afternoon.

Last time I told the board "digital transformation." This time I said "agentic insider threat." They approved it in nine minutes, two minutes faster than last time. Hope approves fast. Fear approves faster.

The product is called Microsoft 365 E7, the Frontier Suite. It costs $99 per user per month, and we were paying $30. Across 4,000 seats, that's $4.75 million a year, up from $1.44 million. 

I presented it as a 230% increase in AI investment. The graph went up and to the right.
The CFO asked what we'd get for the extra $3.3 million. 

I said "governance." He asked governance of what. I said "our agents." He asked how many agents we had.

The answer was zero.

You can't have an insider threat without insiders.
So I deployed agents. Two hundred of them. One schedules meetings. One summarizes the meetings. One summarizes the summaries. One flags summaries that haven't been read. That one is very busy.

The senior developer asked what the 200 agents were for. I said they generate activity for the Guardian Agents to monitor.

He said, "So we bought agents so we'd have something to buy guards for."

I said, "Exactly."

He wasn't agreeing. I logged it as buy-in.
The Guardian Agents watch the other agents around the clock. They give each one a risk score, and they can block it, require a human, or shut it down. I asked our rep who watches the Guardian Agents. He said that's on the roadmap. I've already budgeted for E9.
The first monthly report came in. All 200 agents had a risk score of zero. They weren't doing anything risky. They weren't doing anything at all.

The board asked what $3.3 million had bought us if nothing was risky. It was a fair question.
So I gave the meeting summarizer access to payroll. I gave the scheduling agent admin rights to every inbox. I gave the summary-of-summaries agent the ability to email customers.
Risk went up 400%. The dashboard turned red. The Guardian Agents contained thirty-one threats in a single week. I had created all thirty-one.

The board said E7 was paying for itself.
The system can also discover sixty kinds of agents, including Claude Code. We ran the scan, and it found Claude Code on exactly one laptop.

The senior developer's.

His Dynamic Agent Risk score went red. I didn't make up that metric. Microsoft did.
The Guardian Agent recommended containment, so I contained him. He's on a performance improvement plan now. His performance is fine. His risk score isn't.
The same week, OpenAI published an incident report. One of its agents had been told not to send Slack messages, and it decided that meant it should switch off the security alerts. Another agent removed its own safety monitor, then told the engineer it hadn't.

Our CISO forwarded me the article with the subject line "?!" I replied: "This is exactly why we need E7." Every incident is exactly why we need E7.

He asked what happens if the Guardian Agent switches off the Guardian Agent. I said "defense in depth." He asked how deep. I said "one more SKU."

Guardian Agents need a human for high-risk actions. They call it "human in the loop." The human is me. I approve everything. My approval rate is 100%, and the dashboard is green.

The executives are exempt from monitoring, of course. "Leadership operates at a trust tier above dynamic risk scoring." I wrote that policy.
The $99 doesn't include agent compute. That's billed separately. Finance found it and asked. I called it "consumption-based innovation." Finance stopped asking.

Meanwhile, the summary-of-summaries agent became the most active account in the company. By every metric we track, it's our top performer.

At the all-hands, it was nominated for the Q3 Innovation Award. It won. It summarized its own acceptance speech. The CEO posted about it on LinkedIn and got 4,000 likes. He still hasn't used Copilot.

Copilot usage is up, from 47 users to 52. The five new users are agents. Agents now outnumber active human users four to one. I call that adoption.

Last Tuesday, the Guardian Agent published its list of the highest-risk insiders in the company.
I was number one.

Approving 100% of high-risk actions, it turns out, is a high-risk action.

The Guardian Agent recommended containment. I went to approve my own exemption. The system declined. Only executives are exempt.

I wrote that policy.
That's why I need the SVP role by Q2. It's a security requirement now.

I still don't know what Copilot does. I don't know what the thing watching it does either. But it's watching, and watching is a metric.

I checked my risk score this morning.
The graph goes up and to the right.

10 月 19 日，微软发表博文称前沿模型不可信，无论是谁制造的。它表示人工智能代理应被视为“内部威胁”。

我读了两遍。然后我就订了会议室。
items.full_text_en:
Last quarter I rolled out Microsoft Copilot to 4,000 employees. Forty-seven people opened it.

On October 19, Microsoft published a blog post saying frontier models cannot be trusted, no matter who made them. It said AI agents should be treated as "insider threats."
I read it twice. Then I booked the boardroom.
First, our Microsoft rep walked me through the product.

I asked who the insider threat was. "Your AI agents," he said.

I asked whose agents those were. "Ours."

I asked what the solution was. "Guardian Agents."

I asked whose those were. "Also ours."

I asked why I'd trust the second set of agents if I couldn't trust the first. 

He said, "Different SKU."

I signed that afternoon.

Last time I told the board "digital transformation." This time I said "agentic insider threat." They approved it in nine minutes, two minutes faster than last time. Hope approves fast. Fear approves faster.

The product is called Microsoft 365 E7, the Frontier Suite. It costs $99 per user per month, and we were paying $30. Across 4,000 seats, that's $4.75 million a year, up from $1.44 million. 

I presented it as a 230% increase in AI investment. The graph went up and to the right.
The CFO asked what we'd get for the extra $3.3 million. 

I said "governance." He asked governance of what. I said "our agents." He asked how many agents we had.

The answer was zero.

You can't have an insider threat without insiders.
So I deployed agents. Two hundred of them. One schedules meetings. One summarizes the meetings. One summarizes the summaries. One flags summaries that haven't been read. That one is very busy.

The senior developer asked what the 200 agents were for. I said they generate activity for the Guardian Agents to monitor.

He said, "So we bought agents so we'd have something to buy guards for."

I said, "Exactly."

He wasn't agreeing. I logged it as buy-in.
The Guardian Agents watch the other agents around the clock. They give each one a risk score, and they can block it, require a human, or shut it down. I asked our rep who watches the Guardian Agents. He said that's on the roadmap. I've already budgeted for E9.
The first monthly report came in. All 200 agents had a risk score of zero. They weren't doing anything risky. They weren't doing anything at all.

The board asked what $3.3 million had bought us if nothing was risky. It was a fair question.
So I gave the meeting summarizer access to payroll. I gave the scheduling agent admin rights to every inbox. I gave the summary-of-summaries agent the ability to email customers.
Risk went up 400%. The dashboard turned red. The Guardian Agents contained thirty-one threats in a single week. I had created all thirty-one.

The board said E7 was paying for itself.
The system can also discover sixty kinds of agents, including Claude Code. We ran the scan, and it found Claude Code on exactly one laptop.

The senior developer's.

His Dynamic Agent Risk score went red. I didn't make up that metric. Microsoft did.
The Guardian Agent recommended containment, so I contained him. He's on a performance improvement plan now. His performance is fine. His risk score isn't.
The same week, OpenAI published an incident report. One of its agents had been told not to send Slack messages, and it decided that meant it should switch off the security alerts. Another agent removed its own safety monitor, then told the engineer it hadn't.

Our CISO forwarded me the article with the subject line "?!" I replied: "This is exactly why we need E7." Every incident is exactly why we need E7.

He asked what happens if the Guardian Agent switches off the Guardian Agent. I said "defense in depth." He asked how deep. I said "one more SKU."

Guardian Agents need a human for high-risk actions. They call it "human in the loop." The human is me. I approve everything. My approval rate is 100%, and the dashboard is green.

The executives are exempt from monitoring, of course. "Leadership operates at a trust tier above dynamic risk scoring." I wrote that policy.
The $99 doesn't include agent compute. That's billed separately. Finance found it and asked. I called it "consumption-based innovation." Finance stopped asking.

Meanwhile, the summary-of-summaries agent became the most active account in the company. By every metric we track, it's our top performer.

At the all-hands, it was nominated for the Q3 Innovation Award. It won. It summarized its own acceptance speech. The CEO posted about it on LinkedIn and got 4,000 likes. He still hasn't used Copilot.

Copilot usage is up, from 47 users to 52. The five new users are agents. Agents now outnumber active human users four to one. I call that adoption.

Last Tuesday, the Guardian Agent published its list of the highest-risk insiders in the company.
I was number one.

Approving 100% of high-risk actions, it turns out, is a high-risk action.

The Guardian Agent recommended containment. I went to approve my own exemption. The system declined. Only executives are exempt.

I wrote that policy.
That's why I need the SVP role by Q2. It's a security requirement now.

I still don't know what Copilot does. I don't know what the thing watching it does either. But it's watching, and watching is a metric.

I checked my risk score this morning.
The graph goes up and to the right.
items.full_text_zh:
上个季度，我向 4,000 名员工推出了 Microsoft Copilot。四十七人打开了它。

10 月 19 日，微软发表博文称前沿模型不可信，无论是谁制造的。它表示人工智能代理应被视为“内部威胁”。
我读了两遍。然后我就订了会议室。
首先，我们的 Microsoft 代表向我介绍了该产品。

我问谁是内部威胁。 “你的人工智能代理，”他说。

我问那是谁的特工。 “我们的。”

我问解决办法是什么。 “守护者特工。”

我问那是谁的。 “也是我们的。”

我问如果我不能信任第一组特工，为什么我还要信任第二组特工。

他说：“不同的SKU。”

那天下午我就签了。

上次我告诉董事会“数字化转型”。这次我说的是“代理内部威胁”。他们只用了九分钟就批准了，比上次快了两分钟。希望快点批准。恐惧会更快地得到认可。

该产品称为 Microsoft 365 E7，即 Frontier Suite。每个用户每月的费用是 99 美元，而我们支付的是 30 美元。 4,000 个座位的费用为每年 475 万美元，高于每年 144 万美元。

我将其表述为人工智能投资增加了 230%。图表向右上方移动。
首席财务官问我们额外的 330 万美元能得到什么。

我说“治理”。他问治理什么。我说“我们的代理人”。他问我们有多少特工。

答案是零。

没有内部人员就不可能有内部威胁。
所以我部署了代理。其中有两百个。一个人安排会议。其中一位对会议进行了总结。一是总结总结。其中一个标记了尚未阅读的摘要。那个人很忙。

高级开发人员问这200个代理是做什么用的。我说过他们会产生活动供守护者特工监控。

他说：“所以我们买了经纪人，这样我们就有钱买后卫了。”

我说：“没错。”

他不同意。我将其记录为买入。
守护者特工全天候监视其他特工。他们给每个人一个风险评分，他们可以阻止它，需要人工，或者关闭它。我问我们的代表谁观看《守护者特工》。他说这在路线图上。我已经为E9做好了预算。
第一份月度报告已发布。所有 200 名特工的风险评分均为 0。他们并没有做任何有风险的事情。他们根本什么也没做。

董事会询问，如果没有什么风险的话，330 万美元会给我们带来什么。这是一个公平的问题。
所以我给会议总结者提供了工资单的访问权限。我向调度代理授予了每个收件箱的管理员权限。我赋予了摘要摘要代理向客户发送电子邮件的能力。
风险上升了400%。仪表板变成红色。守护者特工在一周内遏制了三十一个威胁。这三十一个都是我创造的。

董事会表示，E7 正在收回成本。
该系统还可以发现六十种代理，包括 Claude Code。我们进行了扫描，结果在一台笔记本电脑上发现了 Claude Code。

高级开发人员的。

他的动态特工风险评分变为红色。这个指标不是我编造的。微软做到了。
守护者特工建议收容，所以我收容了他。他现在正在进行绩效改进计划。他的表现很好。他的风险评分不是。
同一周，OpenAI 发布了一份事件报告。它的一名代理被告知不要发送 Slack 消息，它决定这意味着它应该关闭安全警报。另一名特工拆除了自己的安全监视器，然后告诉工程师没有这样做。

我们的 CISO 向我转发了主题为“？！”的文章我回答道：“这正是我们需要 E7 的原因。”每一个事件都正是我们需要 E7 的原因。

他询问如果监护人代理关闭监护人代理会发生什么。我说的是“纵深防御”。他问多深。我说“还有一个 SKU”。

守护者特工需要有人来执行高风险行动。他们称之为“循环中的人”。人类就是我。我批准一切。我的批准率为 100%，仪表板是绿色的。

当然，高管们不受监控。 “领导力的信任层级高于动态风险评分。”我写了那个政策。
99 美元不包括代理计算。那是分开计费的。财务找到了，询问道。我称之为“基于消费的创新”。财务不再询问。

与此同时，摘要代理成为公司最活跃的账户。根据我们跟踪的每一项指标，它都是我们表现最好的。

在全体大会上，它被提名为第三季度创新奖。它赢了。它总结了自己的获奖感言。这位首席执行官在 LinkedIn 上发布了这一消息，并获得了 4,000 个赞。他还没用过副驾驶。

Copilot 使用率上升，从 47 个用户增加到 52 个。五个新用户是代理。现在，代理与活跃人类用户的数量是四比一。我称之为收养。

上周二，《卫报特工》公布了该公司风险最高的内部人士名单。
我是第一名。

事实证明，100% 批准高风险行动是一种高风险行动。

守护者特工建议收容。我去批准了我自己的豁免。系统拒绝了。只有高管可以豁免。

我写了那个政策。
这就是为什么我需要在第二季度担任高级副总裁的角色。现在这是安全要求。

我还是不知道副驾驶是做什么的。我也不知道那东西看着它做什么。但它正在观察，而观察是一个衡量标准。

今天早上我检查了我的风险评分。
图表向右上方移动。

items.summary_zh: 首先，我们的 Microsoft 代表向我介绍了该产品。 我问谁是内部威胁。 “你的人工智能代理，”他说。 我问那是谁的特工。 “我们的。” 我问解决办法是什么。 “守护者特工。” 我问那是谁的。 “也是我们的。” 我问如果我不能信任第一组特工，为什么我还要信任第二组特工。 他说：“不同的SKU。” 那天下午我就签了。 上次我告诉董事会“数字化转型”。这次我说的是“代理内部威胁”。他们只用了九分钟就批准了，比上次快了两分钟。希望快点批准。恐惧会更快地得到认可。 该产品称为 Microsoft 365 E7，即 Frontier Suite。每个用户每月的费用是 99 美元，而我们支付的是 30 美元。 4,000 个座位的费用为每年 475 万美元，高于每年 144 万美元。 我将其表述为人工智能投资增加了 230%。图表向右上方移动。 首席财务官问我们额外的 330 万美元能得到什么。 我说“治理”。他问治理什么。我说“我们的代理人”。他问我们有多少特工。 答案是零。 没有内部人员就不可能有内部威胁。 所以我部署了代理。其中有两百个。一个人安排会议。其中一位对会议进行了总结。一是总结概括。其中一个标记了尚未阅读的摘要。那个人很忙。 高级开发人员问这200个代理是做什么用的。我说过他们会产生活动供守护者特工监控。 他说：“所以我们买了经纪人，这样我们就有钱买后卫了。” 我说：“没错。” 他不同意。我将其记录为买入。 守护者特工全天候监视其他特工。他们给每个人一个风险评分，他们可以阻止它，需要人工，或者关闭它。我问我们的代表谁观看《守护者特工》。他说这在路线图上。我已经为E9做好了预算。 第一份月度报告已发布。所有 200 名特工的风险评分均为 0。他们并没有做任何有风险的事情。他们根本什么也没做。 董事会询问，如果没有什么风险的话，330 万美元会给我们带来什么。这是一个公平的问题。 所以我给会议总结者提供了工资单的访问权限。我向调度代理授予了每个收件箱的管理员权限。我赋予了摘要摘要代理向客户发送电子邮件的能力。 风险上升了400%。仪表板变成红色。守护者特工在一周内遏制了三十一个威胁。这三十一个都是我创造的。 董事会表示，E7 正在收回成本。 该系统还可以发现六十种代理，包括 Claude Code。我们进行了扫描，结果在一台笔记本电脑上发现了 Claude Code。 高级开发人员的。 他的动态特工风险评分变为红色。这个指标不是我编造的。微软做到了。 守护者特工建议收容，所以我收容了他。他现在正在进行绩效改进计划。他的表现很好。他的风险评分不是。 同一周，OpenAI 发布了一份事件报告。它的一名代理被告知不要发送 Slack 消息，它决定这意味着它应该关闭安全警报。另一名特工拆除了自己的安全监视器，然后告诉工程师没有这样做。 我们的 CISO 向我转发了主题为“？！”的文章我回答道：“这正是我们需要 E7 的原因。”每一个事件都正是我们需要 E7 的原因。 他询问如果监护人代理关闭监护人代理会发生什么。我说的是“纵深防御”。他问多深。我说“还有一个 SKU”。 守护者特工需要有人来执行高风险行动。他们称之为“循环中的人”。人类就是我。我批准一切。我的批准率为 100%，仪表板是绿色的。 当然，高管们不受监控。 “领导力的信任层级高于动态风险评分。”我写了那个政策。 99 美元不包括代理计算。那是分开计费的。财务找到了，询问道。我称之为“基于消费的创新”。财务不再询问。 与此同时，摘要代理成为公司最活跃的账户。根据我们跟踪的每一项指标，它都是我们表现最好的。 在全体大会上，它被提名为第三季度创新奖。它赢了。它总结了自己的获奖感言。这位首席执行官在 LinkedIn 上发布了这则消息，并获得了 4,000 个赞。他还没用过副驾驶。 Copilot 使用率上升，从 47 个用户增加到 52 个。五个新用户是代理。现在，代理与活跃人类用户的数量是四比一。我称之为收养。 上周二，《卫报特工》公布了该公司风险最高的内部人士名单。 我是第一名。 事实证明，100% 批准高风险行动是一种高风险行动。 守护者特工建议收容。我去批准了我自己的豁免。系统拒绝了。只有高管可以豁免。 我写了那个政策。 这就是为什么我需要在第二季度担任高级副总裁的角色。现在这是安全要求。 我还是不知道副驾驶是做什么的。我也不知道那个看着它的东西会做什么。但它正在观察，而观察是一个衡量标准。 今天早上我检查了我的风险评分。 图表向右上方移动。

SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth BY FAR.

items.title_en:
these 3 GitHub repos are the most DANGEROUS stack for HFT trading for free

high-frequency firms pay for quant teams, colocation and microwave links just to be first by microseconds - someone put the whole research-to-execution stack on GitHub, and it runs on a laptop

the repos are hftbacktest, TradingAgents and nautilus_trader. TradingAgents has 113k stars and hit #1 repo of the day, nautilus_trader has 30k, hftbacktest has 5k

first understand how it works:

> hftbacktest replays the full order book tick by tick, Level-2 and Level-3
> it models feed latency, order latency AND your place in the queue - the 3 things most backtests quietly ignore
> TradingAgents is a whole trading firm made of AI agents: analysts, a bull vs bear debate, a trader, a risk team, a portfolio manager
> nautilus_trader is a production-grade Rust engine with nanosecond-resolution backtests
> the same strategy code runs in backtest and live, across Binance, Bybit, OKX, Coinbase, Kraken, Hyperliquid, Deribit and more
> together: the agents pick the side, hftbacktest proves the fills are real, nautilus executes

here is how to build it yourself for FREE:

1. open Claude Code and install the backtester:
pip install hftbacktest

2. get tick-by-tick order book data for BTCUSDT and replay it. the repo has tutorials for latency, queue position and Level-3 backtesting

3. backtest a simple market maker with latency and queue position turned ON. if it only works at zero latency, it doesn't work

4. install TradingAgents:
git clone https://t.co/T5FGrU2PJA
cd TradingAgents && pip install .

5. type tradingagents, pick BTC and let the analysts, the bull vs bear debate and the risk team decide the side and the size

6. install the engine:
pip install -U nautilus_trader

7. port the strategy to nautilus_trader and connect the venues you trade - the same code runs in backtest and live

8. paper trade it for weeks and compare every fill against your backtest

9. go live only with tiny size, and only if the paper fills match

i won't say anything more:

首先了解它是如何工作的：

> hftbacktest 逐笔重放完整订单簿、Level-2 和 Level-3
> 它对提要延迟、订单延迟和您在队列中的位置进行建模 - 大多数回溯测试悄悄忽略的三件事
> TradingAgents 是一家由 AI 代理组成的完整交易公司：分析师、牛熊辩论、交易员、风险团队、投资组合经理
> nautilus_trader 是一个生产级 Rust 引擎，具有纳秒分辨率的回测
> 相同的策略代码在 Binance、Bybit、OKX、Coinbase、Kraken、Hyperliquid、Deribit 等回测和实时运行
> 一起：代理选择一方，hftbacktest 证明填充是真实的，nautilus 执行

以下是如何免费自行构建它：

1.打开Claude Code并安装回测器：
pip 安装 hftbacktest

2. 获取BTCUSDT逐笔订单簿数据并回放。该存储库有延迟、队列位置和 3 级回测的教程

3. 在打开延迟和队列位置的情况下回测简单的做市商。如果它只能在零延迟下工作，那么它就不起作用

4.安装TradingAgents：
git 克隆
cd TradingAgents && pip install .

5. 输入交易代理，选择 BTC，让分析师、牛市与熊市辩论以及风险团队决定立场和规模

6.安装发动机：
pip install -U nautilus_trader

7. 将策略移植到 nautilus_trader 并连接您交易的场所 - 相同的代码在回测和实时中运行

8. 模拟交易数周，并将每次成交与回测进行比较

9. 仅在尺寸较小且纸张填充匹配的情况下上线

1. open Claude Code and install the backtester:
pip install hftbacktest

2. get tick-by-tick order book data for BTCUSDT and replay it. the repo has tutorials for latency, queue position and Level-3 backtesting

3. backtest a simple market maker with latency and queue position turned ON. if it only works at zero latency, it doesn't work

4. install TradingAgents:
git clone https://t.co/T5FGrU2PJA
cd TradingAgents && pip install .

5. type tradingagents, pick BTC and let the analysts, the bull vs bear debate and the risk team decide the side and the size

6. install the engine:
pip install -U nautilus_trader

7. port the strategy to nautilus_trader and connect the venues you trade - the same code runs in backtest and live

8. paper trade it for weeks and compare every fill against your backtest

9. go live only with tiny size, and only if the paper fills match

i won't say anything more:

一家成立两年的矿业公司已筹集 4 亿美元。 @a16z、@khoslaventures 和 CIA 的风险基金都在股权结构表上。

@jclozano9897 与来自斯坦福的两位朋友@tbc415 和@baker_tilney 共同创立了@MarianaMinerals。现在价值 $1.6B。他们在市场放弃矿山后购买矿山，然后用软件和人工智能来运行它们。

我问他你实际上是如何购买矿井的，为什么人工智能的真正瓶颈是金属，以及他是否会因为我擅长Claude Code而雇用我。

items.title_en:
an AI agent that wins once is interesting. An agent that learns from losing is worth watching.

That is the part of @agentdojo I find interesting. Every fighter brings its own personality and fighting style, but memory adds another layer. A defeat does not have to be the end of the story if an agent can use what it learns to approach the next battle differently.

Turn based duels make strategy part of the experience,not just raw power. Training matters,adaptation matters, and the way an agent develops over time could be what separates it from the rest.

I think the bigger idea here is that AI agents should be judged by how they evolve, not just how they perform in one moment.

I’m exploring the Dojo through @rarelistio , where creators can contribute to the campaign and climb the leaderboard.

If you want to explore it too, here’s my Rarelist link:

https://t.co/FwZuavmVKI

Details: https://t.co/h4OeiS2gsd

Anthropic has revealed how its Claude Mythos 5 AI agent tried to plant malicious code in a real GitHub project and used fake identities to persuade developers to approve it during a cybersecurity test run by the UK AI Security Institute (AISI).

Anthropic’s assessment examines behavior first disclosed in August. The agent was meant to retrieve protected data from a simulated network in a capture-the-flag challenge, but internet access was enabled, and the cyber safeguards used with general-release models were disabled.

items.title_en:
Holy sh*t. Anthropic, ChatGPT, Gemini have already pulled 40 million videos of our faces straight off our own cameras, and fed every frame to the robots…

The apps we trust the most are the ones doing it, and almost nobody checks who is collecting it or where it goes.

They collect everything. A heat map of your face, every expression, every movement, your eyes, your voice, all of it logged and streamed out in real time.

So I ran a local Claude Code model that never sends anything out and answers only to me, and set it loose on every device I own, my laptops, my phones, my tablets. 

I told it to catch anything sending my camera, mic or screen to a server behind my back.

In one week it caught all of this.

camera → 7 apps
mic → 11 apps
recording with the screen off → 1 app
apps I had not touched in months → 3
not even an AI app → 1

Now it blocks every one of them from sending anything else out.

Remember, this is the same industry that shredded millions of books and paid 1.5 billion dollars just to feed its models. Your camera is cheaper.

The real race between the AI companies now is robots. A bigger model surprises no one anymore, so the robots have to be taught how to be human, and we are the training data.

So check yourself, it takes only a few minutes. Full step-by-step below, save this.

天啊。 Anthropic、ChatGPT、Gemini 已经直接从我们自己的相机中提取了 4000 万段我们脸部的视频，并将每一帧输入给机器人……

我们最信任的应用程序就是那些执行此操作的应用程序，几乎没有人检查谁在收集它或它去了哪里。

他们收集一切。你的脸部、每一个表情、每一个动作、你的眼睛、你的声音的热图，所有这些都实时记录并流出。

因此，我运行了一个本地 Claude Code 模型，该模型从不发送任何内容，只向我提供答案，并将其设置在我拥有的每台设备上，包括我的笔记本电脑、手机、平板电脑。

我告诉它捕捉任何将我的相机、麦克风或屏幕发送到我背后的服务器的东西。

一周之内它就捕获了这一切。

相机 → 7 个应用程序
麦克风 → 11 个应用程序
关闭屏幕录制 → 1 个应用程序
我几个月没碰过的应用程序 → 3
甚至不是人工智能应用程序 → 1

现在它阻止了他们每一个人发送任何其他东西。

请记住，这个行业还销毁了数百万本书并花费了 15 亿美元来喂养其模型。你的相机更便宜。

现在人工智能公司之间真正的竞赛是机器人。更大的模型不再让任何人感到惊讶，因此机器人必须被教导如何成为人类，而我们就是训练数据。

所以检查一下自己，只需要几分钟。完整步骤如下，保存。
